Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: The profile otherwise reflects fear, vigilance, avoidance of proximity/anger cues, and beliefs that others may harm her. In that context, endorsing risky or self-endangering behavior is hard to reconcile clinically, especially with no Maladaptive Strategies items or other disinhibition/externalising content to support it.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: For intimate partner physical abuse, a global appraisal that 'you can never know who will harm you' is possible but sits somewhat awkwardly beside highly specific interpersonal triggers (physical proximity, others' anger) and trauma-linked memory content. It implies diffuse unpredictability of all potential perpetrators rather than the more coherent expected pattern of threat from close others or angry interpersonal situations.

vignette: Ella, a 77-year-old African American woman and former politician, has been living with the haunting memories of physical abuse inflicted by her romantic partner over two decades ago. Despite the years that have passed since the traumatic event, Ella’s daily life is marred by a series of interconnected fears and flashbacks that keep the trauma vividly alive. The night was particularly harrowing for Ella; she had been dozing off when a loud bang jolted her awake, leaving her feeling jumpy and easily startled. This startle response has become a constant companion, making it difficult for her to feel safe at any time of day or night. Her husband noticed the change in her — how she would often look behind her, as if expecting someone to follow closely. The physical proximity of others, even those she once trusted, now triggers a deep sense of unease. Ella’s memory of the event is fragmented; she feels like only parts are clear while the rest remain hazy or blocked before they can be fully recalled. Each time she tries to piece together what happened, intense guilt floods her, as if every incomplete fragment represents a failure on her part. This guilt deepens her belief that she has permanently changed for the worse and will never feel normal emotions again. The thought of this permanent damage is overwhelming, reinforcing her mistrust in others and making her question whether people can be trusted at all. In the context of her work as a politician, Ella’s avoidance behaviors have become increasingly evident. She avoids public forums where she might encounter expressions of anger from constituents, even when conveyed calmly. Her fear that any display of anger could reignite the traumatic memories has led to frequent absences from key meetings and events. This avoidance has strained her relationships with colleagues who no longer understand why she seems distant or disengaged. The visual cues of blood have also become potent triggers for Ella. A recent incident where she witnessed a minor accident on television triggered a flashback, leaving her feeling acutely vulnerable. These flashbacks make it harder for her to trust others and heighten her vigilance at night, when the darkness seems to magnify her fears. Ella’s narrative of the traumatic event is one of sustained abuse that culminated in a particularly violent incident where she was physically assaulted by her partner. The memory of blood and the fear instilled during these moments make even minor triggers potent reminders of the past. As she recalls these events, she feels like she can never fully remember what happened, pushing away parts of the memory before they are complete. The cycle of fear is relentless for Ella. Her negative appraisals that she has been permanently damaged and mistrust others fuel her heightened startle response and vigilance. This vigilant state then exacerbates her fragmented memories and intensifies her feelings of guilt and loss. The more she dwells on the incomplete picture of what happened, the more it reinforces her belief in the permanence of her trauma. What finally brought Ella to seek help was a combination of her husband’s growing concern over her mental health and the realization that she could no longer ignore how deeply the memories were impacting her daily life. She is most afraid of never fully recovering from this trauma, but hopes for a chance at reclaiming her sense of safety and trust in others.
